tips.title: Wash your panels the smart way
tips.body: Rinse with plain water early in the morning or at sunset. Never splash cold water on hot glass at midday, and skip soap and hard brushes.
tips.more: Lebanese dust and pollen settle fast, especially after a dry spell or a sandstorm. A gentle rinse every few weeks keeps output up. A soft mop with a long handle is enough; abrasive pads scratch the anti-reflective coating.

tips.title: Run heavy loads between 10:00 and 15:00
tips.body: Washing machine, water pump, electric heater, ironing: schedule them while the sun is high and your panels are at their peak.
tips.more: Every kWh you use straight from the panels is a kWh your battery doesn't have to store and your generator doesn't have to make. Timers and smart plugs make this automatic.

tips.title: Don't empty your battery every night
tips.body: Keep a reserve of about 20% in a lithium battery. Deep daily discharges shorten its life.
tips.more: Most hybrid inverters let you set a minimum state of charge. Ask your installer to set a sensible cut-off so the battery always has a buffer for the morning and for cloudy days.

tips.title: One shadow can cost a whole string
tips.body: A water tank, antenna or satellite dish shading a single panel can pull down the output of every panel wired with it.
tips.more: Panels in a string behave like a chain: the weakest link sets the pace. Before installing, walk the roof at 9:00, 12:00 and 15:00 and note every shadow. Move small obstacles if you can.

tips.title: Check your app, not just your lights
tips.body: Compare today's kWh with a similar sunny day. A sudden drop usually means dust, new shade or a fault.
tips.more: Your inverter app keeps daily and monthly history. A quick look once a week catches problems early, before they cost you weeks of lost production.

tips.title: Hot panels make less power
tips.body: Solar panels lose roughly 0.3 to 0.4% of output for every degree above 25°C. Spring often beats midsummer.
tips.more: That is why a bright, cool April day can produce as much as a hot August one. Good airflow behind the panels helps them stay cooler.

tips.title: Expect less in winter, and plan for it
tips.body: In Lebanon, a December day gives roughly half the energy of a July day: the sun is lower and the days are shorter.
tips.more: Size your system and your habits for winter, not only for summer. Shift loads to midday, and keep the generator for the gaps.

tips.title: Size the battery for your nights
tips.body: List what must run after sunset: fridge, lights, router, TV, a fan. That list sizes your battery, not your whole bill.
tips.more: Daytime loads should run directly on the panels. A battery sized for the evening and night keeps the investment reasonable and the battery working within its comfort zone.

tips.title: Give your inverter room to breathe
tips.body: Keep the inverter out of direct sun and out of closed cupboards. Heat makes it reduce its output.
tips.more: Leave clearance around the unit as the manual specifies, keep the fins dust-free, and never stack boxes against it.

tips.title: An old fridge can cost you panels
tips.body: An inefficient fridge can use double the energy of a modern inverter model. Replacing it can be cheaper than adding panels.
tips.more: Check the energy label. Fridges run day and night, so they matter most for your battery. Keep the door seals clean and the back coil dusted.

tips.title: Heat water with the midday sun
tips.body: Put the electric water heater on a timer for late morning and early afternoon, or use a solar thermal heater.
tips.more: A tank heated at noon stays warm into the evening. A solar thermal collector is still the cheapest way to heat water in Lebanon.

tips.title: Solar and the generator can be friends
tips.body: Ask your installer to set the generator charging current so the generator is never overloaded.
tips.more: Hybrid inverters can charge the battery from the generator. A correct limit protects both machines and avoids the generator tripping when the house is also drawing power.

tips.title: After a storm, look but don't touch
tips.body: Check for cracked glass, loose cables or moved panels. Panel cables are live whenever there is daylight.
tips.more: Even the switched-off panel side can carry dangerous DC voltage. If something looks wrong, switch off at the inverter and call your installer.

tips.title: Know where your DC switch is
tips.body: The DC isolator disconnects the panels from the inverter. Every adult in the house should know where it is.
tips.more: Ask your installer to label the DC isolator, the AC breaker and the battery breaker clearly. In an emergency, seconds count.

tips.title: Keep your paperwork
tips.body: Panel performance warranties typically run 25 to 30 years, inverters 5 to 10. Keep invoices and serial numbers.
tips.more: Photograph the labels on panels, inverter and battery on installation day and keep them with the invoice. Warranty claims are much easier with proof.

tips.title: The right tilt for Lebanon
tips.body: For a fixed system facing south, a tilt of about 25 to 30° is a good all-year compromise at Lebanon's latitude.
tips.more: Steeper favours winter, flatter favours summer. Most homes are best served by the all-year compromise.

tips.title: East–west roofs still work
tips.body: Panels facing east and west produce somewhat less than south-facing ones, but spread production over a longer day.
tips.more: That flatter curve can suit homes with morning and evening loads, and it often fits more panels on the roof.

tips.title: The 1 kWp yardstick
tips.body: In Lebanon, each 1 kWp of well-installed panels produces roughly 1,500 to 1,650 kWh a year.
tips.more: Use it as a sanity check on any offer. Divide your yearly consumption by this figure to get a first idea of the system size you need.

tips.title: Put the battery in a cool place
tips.body: Install batteries in a ventilated, shaded spot away from bedrooms. Heat ages every battery.
tips.more: LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) is the safer and longer-lasting chemistry for homes. Keep the area clear and dry.

tips.title: Hunt the standby drain
tips.body: A device drawing 20 W around the clock uses about 0.5 kWh a day, straight from your battery at night.
tips.more: Old receivers, chargers and decoders left on standby add up. Use switched power strips for the TV corner and the office.

tips.title: Design Voc for the coldest morning
tips.body: Voc rises as cells get colder. Correct string Voc to the site's minimum temperature and stay under the inverter's max DC input.
tips.more: Use the module's Voc temperature coefficient (typically around −0.25 to −0.3 %/°C). Mountain sites in Lebanon can see sub-zero winter mornings, which pushes Voc well above STC.

tips.title: Check Vmp at hot cell temperature
tips.body: At a summer cell temperature of around 70°C, the string Vmp must still sit inside the inverter's MPPT window.
tips.more: Too few modules per string and the hot-day voltage drops below the tracker's minimum, so the inverter loses the MPP exactly when irradiance is highest.

tips.title: One MPPT, one orientation, one module
tips.body: Don't mix module models, tilts or azimuths on the same MPPT input. Mismatch costs yield.
tips.more: Use separate MPPT inputs for east and west arrays, or for strings with different module counts.

tips.title: Keep DC voltage drop under about 1.5%
tips.body: Size DC cables for voltage drop, not just ampacity. UV-rated solar cable, 4 or 6 mm² for most residential strings.
tips.more: Long roof-to-basement runs are common in Lebanese buildings. Calculate the drop for the full loop length (go and return).

tips.title: Never mix MC4 brands
tips.body: Mated connectors from different manufacturers are a classic cause of hot joints and fires. Same brand, proper crimp tool.
tips.more: Cross-mated connectors void warranties and can fail open-circuit or overheat. Crimp, don't solder, and pull-test every joint.

tips.title: Battery cables carry the big current
tips.body: A 5 kW inverter on a 48 V battery draws over 100 A. Size the cable and fuse or breaker at the battery for that.
tips.more: Undersized battery leads run hot and cause voltage sag and nuisance low-voltage cut-offs. Keep them short, use proper lugs and torque them to spec.

tips.title: Bond the frames, add surge protection
tips.body: Earth module frames and rails, and fit Type 2 SPDs on both the DC and AC sides.
tips.more: Rooftop arrays are exposed to induced surges. Keep earthing conductors short and direct, and check SPD status windows during maintenance.

tips.title: Three or more strings in parallel? Fuse them
tips.body: With three or more parallel strings, a fault can back-feed one string from the others. String fuses prevent it.
tips.more: Check the module's maximum series fuse rating and size the fuses accordingly.

tips.title: Space rows for the winter solstice
tips.body: At Beirut's latitude the noon sun on 21 December is about 33° high. Row gap ≈ 1.55 × the rise of the panel ahead.
tips.more: Rise = panel length × sin(tilt). Add a margin if you want shade-free hours beyond noon in winter.

tips.title: A DC/AC ratio of 1.1 to 1.3 is normal
tips.body: Oversizing the array relative to the inverter raises morning and evening yield, with only small midday clipping.
tips.more: Check the inverter's maximum DC input power and current per MPPT before oversizing.

tips.title: Use BMS communication, not voltage guesses
tips.body: Connect lithium batteries over CAN or RS485 and select the matching battery protocol. SOC becomes accurate.
tips.more: Voltage-based 'user' profiles misread the flat LiFePO4 curve, leading to early cut-offs or overcharging.

tips.title: Charge voltages come from the datasheet
tips.body: For a 16S LiFePO4 pack, absorption is typically around 56 V, but always use the battery maker's values.
tips.more: Wrong charge settings are the fastest way to unbalance cells. Set absorption, float and cut-off exactly as the manufacturer specifies.

tips.title: Scan with a thermal camera
tips.body: After commissioning, an IR scan under good sun reveals hot cells, loose terminals and failing connectors.
tips.more: Repeat the scan once a year. It takes minutes and finds problems that no app will show.

tips.title: Measure every string before connecting
tips.body: Strings on the same MPPT should show Voc within about 2 to 3% of each other.
tips.more: A string reading clearly low usually means a missing module, reversed polarity or a bad connector. Fix it before the inverter sees it.

tips.title: Design for the wind, not the brochure
tips.body: Ballast or anchor to the calculated wind load for the site. Coastal and mountain roofs see very different loads.
tips.more: Check the roof slab and parapets. A short structural note for each site protects the client and the contractor.

tips.title: Check N–PE bonding in battery mode
tips.body: When a hybrid inverter runs off-grid, the neutral–earth bond must be correct, or the RCDs downstream won't work.
tips.more: Many hybrids switch the bond with an internal relay. Test RCD tripping with the grid or generator disconnected.

tips.title: Tune the generator input
tips.body: Set the maximum AC charge current and use the generator mode so the inverter accepts generator frequency swings.
tips.more: Lebanese private generators often drift in frequency and voltage. The right input mode stops the inverter from dropping the generator repeatedly.

tips.title: CT clamp direction matters
tips.body: For zero-export or export limiting, the CT arrow must point the way the manufacturer specifies, usually toward the grid.
tips.more: A reversed CT makes the inverter think the house is exporting while it is importing. Check the live readings at commissioning.

tips.title: Clean with soft water
tips.body: Hard water leaves scale on the glass that cuts light more than the dust you removed. Use soft or demineralised water.
tips.more: Avoid high-pressure jets on edges and junction boxes. Clean when the panels are cool.

tips.title: High altitude? Check the load rating
tips.body: For snowy mountain sites, choose modules and mounting rated for heavy front loads, such as 5,400 Pa.
tips.more: Check the clamping zones in the installation manual; the rated load only applies when the module is clamped where the manufacturer says.
